INTRODUCTION 1 It is important to establish an internationally standardised procedure to ensure the quality of post- 2 approval safety information and to harmonise, where feasible, the way of gathering and reporting 3 information. The ICH E2D guideline provides guidance on definitions and standards for post- 4 approval individual case safety reporting, as well as good case management practices. This 5 guideline was originally based on the content of the ICH E2A guideline (which provides guidance 6 on pre-approval safety data management), with consideration as to how the terms and definitions 7 should be applied in the post-approval phase of the product life cycle. Detailed guidance on the 8 specific structure, format, standards, and data elements for transmitting Individual Case Safety 9 Reports (ICSRs) is provided in the ICH E2B guideline. Guidance on periodic reporting of 10 aggregated safety data is covered in the ICH E2C guideline. 11 This guideline provides recommendations that are harmonised to the extent possible given 12 differences in post-market safety reporting requirements among ICH regions. Where applicable, 13 this guideline notes where local and regional requirements may vary and, as such, marketing 14 authorisation holders (MAHs) should refer to the relevant local or regional regulatory authority’s 15 requirements. 16

candidates.statement: 2.1.4 Unexpected AE/ADR 55 MAHs should treat AEs/ADRs in ICSRs as unexpected if the reported AE/ADR is not included 56 in any section of the local/regional product labelling (e.g., Prescribing Information or 57 Summary of Product Characteristics). In addition, an AE/ADR in an ICSR whose nature, 58 severity, or specificity is not consistent with the term or description used in the local/regional 59 product labelling should be considered unexpected. When an MAH is uncertain whether an 60 AE/ADR in an ICSR for a country or region should be treated as expected or unexpected, the 61 AE/ADR should be treated as unexpected for that local country or region. 62 An ADR included in the local/regional product labelling should be considered unexpected 63 when it is reported with a fatal outcome in an ICSR unless the labelling specifically states that 64 the ADR might be associated with a fatal outcome. 65 Product labelling may include information related to ADRs for the pharmaceutical class to 66 which the medicinal product belongs. This situation is often referred to as ‘‘Class ADRs’’, and 67 such class ADRs should not automatically be considered “expected” when reported in an ICSR 68 for one of the medicinal products. candidates.statement: 2.2 Individual Case Safety Report (ICSR) including Minimum Criteria for Reporting 89 An ICSR is a description of an AE/ADR or other observation in an individual patient at a specific 90 point of time. 91 The minimum criteria for reporting ICSRs are: 92 • At least one AE/ADR – see Section 5.1.1, or other observation – see Section 5.1.3; 93 • At least one suspect or interacting 1 medicinal product; 94 • An identifiable patient – see Section 6.1; 95 • At least one identifiable reporter – see Section 6.1; 96 A case is the information received by an MAH or regulatory authority about an AE/ADR or other 97 observation. Cases missing any of the above criteria do not qualify for reporting; due diligence 98 should be exercised to collect the missing criteria. 99 While these criteria are the minimum needed for a case to be eligible for reporting, regulatory 100 authorities may have additional criteria, as specified by local and regional requirements, for 101 reporting of a case to be required. See Section 5, Standards for Reporting, for more information 102 on what should be reported. 103

candidates.statement: 6.4 Follow-up Information 580 Initial AE/ADR reports may not have sufficient information for clinical case evaluation, and 581 efforts should be made to seek additional information on reports, including AE(s)/ADR(s) that 582 were reported second-hand (i.e., cases where the reporter is aware of an AE/ADR, but does not 583 have first-hand knowledge of relevant information about the event). 584 To optimise the value of follow-up, the first consideration should be prioritisation of case reports 585 by importance. Highest priority for follow-up are cases which are both serious and unexpected. 586 At a slightly lower priority are serious, expected and non-serious, unexpected cases. However, 587 in addition to seriousness and expectedness as criteria, cases ‘‘of special interest’’ (e.g., 588 AEs/ADRs under enhanced monitoring at the request of regulatory authorities) also deserve extra 589 attention. 590 All requests/attempts for follow-up information should be documented. The MAH should provide 591 specific questions it would like to have answered. Follow-up methods should be tailored towards 592 optimising the collection of missing information. 593 To facilitate the capture of clinically relevant and complete information, use of a targeted 594 questionnaire/specific form is encouraged, preferably at the time of the initial report. Individuals 595 with the appropriate level of pharmacovigilance training and therapeutic expertise should be 596 involved in the follow-up of received cases. For serious AEs/ADRs, it is important to continue 597 follow-up and report new information until the outcome has been established or the patient’s 598 condition is stabilised. 599
